title: Say yes to AI context without losing control: a new way to set up and govern connectors in Atlassian Administration
summary: Set up third-party connectors faster, manage them all in one place, and control data and actions across your org with the new connector experience for admins.
body_markdown:
## It’s 9:12 on a Monday, and Maya has a decision to make


Maya runs IT for Beaconstone Financial, a fintech company with 2,000 employees. Her engineering teams work in Jira and GitHub. Sales lives in Salesforce. Most decisions happen in Slack threads, Google Docs, and SharePoint folders that nobody can find six months later.


Leadership wants Rovo to answer questions across all of it. Her head of sales has asked for account briefs that pull in the latest Salesforce opportunity data and last week’s customer call. Her engineering director wants release summaries that link Jira work to the pull requests behind it.


Maya likes the idea. Her CISO has questions first:


*What data leaves those systems? Where does it go? Who can see it? What happens if someone connects a personal Google account? And if something goes wrong at 2 a.m., how quickly can we shut it off?*


Most admins know this conversation well. Interest in AI isn’t what holds rollouts back. **Uncertainty is.** Admins won’t connect business-critical systems until they can answer those questions with evidence.


That’s what the new connector experience in Atlassian Administration is for.


## First, why connect anything at all?


AI is only as useful as the context it can see. A model can write a fluent answer, but if it doesn’t know your customers, your roadmap, or what your team decided in last Tuesday’s thread, that answer is generic.


**Teamwork Graph** is how Atlassian gives AI that context. It maps the relationships between your work: people, teams, goals, projects, work items, pages, and the decisions that connect them. It covers Jira, Confluence, Loom, and the rest of Atlassian’s apps, and **connectors** extend it to the third-party tools where much of your work actually happens: Google Drive, SharePoint, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Salesforce, GitHub, Zendesk, ServiceNow, Zoom, Gong, and many more.


When those tools are connected, Rovo Search, Chat, and Agents can reason across them together:


- **A product manager** asks, *“What did customers say about the new billing flow?”* and gets an answer drawn from Zendesk tickets, a Gong call transcript, and the Jira epic tracking the fix.
- **An engineering lead** gets a release summary that ties Jira work items to the GitHub pull requests that shipped them, without opening either tool.
- **An account executive** preps for a renewal with the Salesforce opportunity, the latest Slack escalation, and the shared SharePoint proposal in one view.


Connected content also keeps the source system’s permissions. People only see what they could already open in the original tool.


The payoff is real, and the admin is the person who makes it happen. So we rebuilt the admin experience around one idea: **governance should be what lets you say yes, not what makes you say “not yet.”**


## What’s new for admins


### 1. Setup that respects your time, and your approval process


**Before:** Maya would start setting up a connector, get three screens in, and find out she needed a service account she didn’t have, a scope only the Google Workspace admin could grant, or a sign-off from security. The half-finished setup disappeared when she closed the tab, and she started from scratch next time.


**Now:** the connector setup flow has been redesigned so admins know exactly what they’re getting into before they start.


**Know what you need before you begin.** Every connector now opens with a clear *Before you begin* summary that lists what setup requires: the admin roles you need in the third-party tool, any service accounts or apps to create, and the permissions to grant. If you need to bring in a Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 admin, you’ll know on the first screen, not the fifth.


**Make an informed decision with an expanded Trust section.** The Trust section brings key security information together and points admins to connector-specific support pages for details that may change. Those pages are the source of truth for the most up-to-date connector information. Admins can use both during their security review to find:


- **Where to find what’s accessed:** the connector-specific support page details the content types and objects the connector reads, such as files, messages, records, or transcripts
- **What permissions are requested:** check the connector-specific support page for current scopes and whether they allow read-only access or actions
- **How data flows:** consult the Trust section and linked support documentation for details on indexing into Teamwork Graph, permissions, and data use
- **Where to find available controls:** the connector-specific support page describes which content, time, and label-based controls are available for that connector before ingestion


Admins can review the Trust section and linked support pages themselves or share them with security and legal to inform their approval process. Refer to the connector-specific support pages for the latest details.


**Save your progress as a draft.** Approvals take time. Now, when you need a missing credential, an answer from security, or a colleague’s sign-off, you can **save the connector as a draft** and come back later. Your settings, including content inclusion and exclusion rules, are kept. Drafts show up in your connector list with a *Draft* label and a **Complete setup** action that takes you straight back to where you stopped. Reminders by email and in-app notification help make sure a draft doesn’t get forgotten. For security, credentials and secrets are never pre-filled; you re-enter them when you finish.


**For Maya,** the Salesforce setup that used to take a week of back-and-forth now looks like this: she reviews the prerequisites on Monday, sends the Trust summary to her CISO, saves a draft, and finishes the connection Wednesday afternoon once approval comes through.


### 2. Every connector, one control center


**Before:** some connectors were installed by admins. Others, like Smart Links and default tools that let Rovo read or act in third-party apps, were available by default and managed somewhere else. Knowing what was connected, how healthy it was, and who was using it meant checking several pages.


**Now:** **Connectors** is a top-level section in Atlassian Administration, with one table for every connector in your organization, both the ones you installed and the default connectors that come with Rovo.


At a glance, the table shows:


Column What it tells you


**Connector and type** Which tool it is, and whether it’s an indexed connector you added or an included connector


**Status** *Connected* , *Syncing* , *Draft* , or **Action required**


**Indexing** Whether content is being indexed into Teamwork Graph, and how many objects have been indexed


**Search** Whether the connector’s content appears in Rovo Search


**Installed by** Who set it up, so you always know who to contact


**Site** Filter by site if you run more than one


**See what needs attention, and fix it.** When a token expires, a permission scope is missing, or a sync fails, the connector is flagged **Action required** with a specific explanation and a next step, such as re-authorizing a connector or granting a missing scope. Problems don’t fail silently anymore; you see them before your users do.


Select any connector to open its detail page, where you manage it end to end.


**Decide exactly what gets indexed.** You choose what content from each tool goes into Teamwork Graph. Controls are layered, and they vary by connector:


- **Folder, site, and channel controls:** allowlist or blocklist specific folders, drives, SharePoint sites, Teams channels, or Slack channels. For example, index the product and support drives but leave out finance and HR.
- **Time-based controls:** only index content created or updated within a time window you set, such as the last 12 months.
- **Object-level controls:** for record-based tools like Salesforce, choose which objects to exclude.


A policy summary on each connector shows which controls are active, so you can check your posture quickly.


**Know it’s working.** The detail page shows indexing status and object counts as content syncs. If someone asks, *“Why can’t Rovo find the Q3 pricing doc?”* , use the **index check** to look up a specific file, page, channel, or record and confirm whether it’s been indexed, and if not, why.


**See who’s connected.** See how many people in your organization have connected their own accounts to each tool, so you can track adoption and spot where teams need a nudge. (available on December 2026)


**Control included connectors and tools too.** Included connectors are now in the same view as everything else. You can see the read and write tools each connector exposes to Rovo, and enable or disable those tools individually or in bulk. If a default connector turns out to be valuable, you can upgrade it to full indexing from the same page.


**For Maya,** the Monday question *“What are we actually connected to?”* now takes 30 seconds. One table, every connector, every status, and a clear list of what needs her attention.


### 3. Only your company’s authorized accounts can connect


**Before:** when people connected their own accounts to a third-party tool, there was nothing stopping them from using a personal account instead of a work account. A personal Google Drive or a side-project GitHub organization could end up in the same workflows as company data. Security teams wanted a way to keep connections on authorized corporate identities.


**Now:** admins can set **authorized email domains** for connectors. Only accounts on the domains you approve, such as your organization’s verified corporate domain, can connect. Personal and unapproved accounts are blocked when someone tries to sign in, and the check happens centrally, so it applies no matter where the connection starts, whether in Rovo Chat, Search, or an agent.


- **Company domains allowed:** add every domain your organization uses, including subsidiaries and acquisitions.
- **Personal accounts blocked:** Gmail, Outlook.com, and other personal or unapproved domains can’t be connected.
- **Clear feedback for users:** anyone who tries to connect an unapproved account sees why it was blocked and what to do.


**For Maya’s CISO,** this was the deciding control. Connected context now stays within corporate identity once you set your authorized domains.


### 4. An org-wide control for when you need to act fast


Most days, connectors just work. But every security team plans for the day something unexpected happens: a vulnerability disclosure from a third-party vendor, a suspicious pattern in the audit log, or an agent doing something nobody intended.


On that day, you shouldn’t have to find and turn off dozens of tools one connector at a time.


**Now:** admins have an **organization-wide control** that blocks **read tools, write tools, or both** across all included third-party connectors, for every Rovo experience.


- **Block write actions only** to stop Rovo from creating, updating, or sending anything in third-party tools, while people can still search and read.
- **Block read and write** to pause all default third-party tool access while you investigate.
- **Your settings are kept.** Connector-level choices you’ve already made are saved. When you turn the org-wide control off, every connector goes back to exactly how you had it configured, so there’s nothing to rebuild.


It’s the difference between a scramble and a plan. You can respond in seconds, investigate calmly, and restore service with one click.


## What this means for your organization


Who What changes


**Admins** Faster setup with no surprises, drafts that fit how approvals really happen, one place to manage every connector, and problems flagged before users notice.


**Security and compliance** Plain-language trust information for every connector, content controls enforced before ingestion, corporate-only account connections, and an org-wide control for incident response.


**IT and business leaders** A repeatable way to roll out AI context across teams, with visibility into what’s connected, what’s healthy, and what’s being used.


**Everyone else** Rovo answers that draw on the tools teams use every day, sooner, with the permissions they expect.


Back at Beaconstone Financial, Maya’s rollout plan went from *“not until we have answers”* to a staged launch: Google Drive and Slack in week one, Salesforce and GitHub in week two, with content controls, authorized domains, and the org-wide control set before the first sync. Her CISO signed off on the rollout.


## Get started


1. **Open Connectors** in[Atlassian Administration](https://admin.atlassian.com/) to see every connector in your organization in one place.
2. **Set your guardrails first:** add your authorized email domains and review the org-wide tool control settings.
3. **Connect one high-value tool.** Pick the one your teams ask about most. Review the *Before you begin* checklist and Trust section, save a draft if you need approval, and apply content controls before you connect.


Then ask Rovo a question you couldn’t answer before.


**[Explore connectors](https://www.atlassian.com/software/rovo/connectors)** · **[Read the admin documentation](https://support.atlassian.com/organization-administration/docs/manage-your-teamwork-graph-connectors/)**
